argument: This episode extends Deleuze and Guattari's rejection of static, individualist perspectives from politics to social theory, introducing the concept of 'flows,' movements of value (economic, of traffic, of ideas) between two poles that machines seek connections with and territorialize. Just as analyzing a river only in terms of the fixed identity of its parts misses the deeper question of what force drives it and how intervention reshapes it, philosophers who prescribe static identities to social phenomena miss that the world is fundamentally in motion. This leads into Deleuze's larger claim that difference, not identity, is prior and foundational, a claim he connects to his own reading of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, which the episode says opens up an entirely new perspective on philosophy's long tradition of dividing the world into being versus becoming — a perspective it leaves for the next episode.
keyIdeas: A flow, first defined economically, is 'the values of the quantities of goods and services or money transmitted from one pole to another'; the concept then expands to traffic, immigration, ideas, and even sewage, since movement occurs at every level of society.

Philosophers analyzing a river (or a flow) by breaking it into parts and assigning each an identity miss what actually matters: the force driving the movement and how human intervention (a dam, a law) reshapes it.
Market regulations and traffic laws are like a dam or a redirected river course: interventions that reterritorialize a flow to meet a demand, becoming part of the flow's identity in that moment.

The wasp that pollinates orchids becomes, in that moment, part of the orchid's reproductive flow rather than a fixed self; the same process of 'becoming' applies to a lobbyist and oil, an individual and traffic, or a movement and the flow of ideas.

Deleuze inverts the traditional assumption that identity precedes difference (a table needs an identity before it can be distinguished from a chair); for him, difference is prior to identity, a claim he ties to his own reading of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, which he takes to call the long-standing being-versus-becoming dichotomy into question — a line of thought the episode says it will develop first thing in the next episode.

terms.def: A value of goods, services, money, people, or ideas moving between two poles; the basic unit Deleuze and Guattari use to analyze social phenomena beyond static identities.

Territorialization is machines intervening in and reshaping a flow (like a dam reshaping a river) to meet some demand, becoming part of the flow's identity; deterritorialization is the opposite movement, where a thing's fixed identity falls away — the pollinating wasp is deterritorialized in that there is no sense of identity given to it from the outside, only the connections it has in that moment.

The long-standing Western philosophical dichotomy between what is constant/unchanging (being) and what is constantly in motion/flux (becoming), which the episode presents as something Deleuze's reading of Nietzsche calls into question.
Deleuze's inversion of the traditional view that things need identities before they can be different; for him, identity is actually derived from difference.

Nietzsche's idea that one should live as if every moment of one's life will repeat identically forever; Deleuze reads it as making a point close to his own, one the episode says leads to a new perspective on being versus becoming.
